items.question: What do you think success in racing comes down to?
items.object: Organization, human-machine collaboration, and data in racing
items.answer: It's always going to be about who can organize the best. The man and the machine—how do you get those to work together as seamlessly as possible? It's when everybody's kind of on the same page that results come from. Data is everything with racing at this point. I believe we are in what's called the data wars right now.

The response characterizes contemporary racing as a competition over data.

items.question: What do you see as distinctive about working with motorsports data?
items.answer: It's a very unique kind of data. It's a lot of high-bandwidth time-series data that we can both look at retroactively, but we also want to be able to process in real time at the track, make calls and draw conclusions as quickly as possible.
quotes: And it's a very unique kind of data.

items.question: What do you want RaceTek Systems’ racing intelligence tools to enable for racing crews?
items.answer: We do have one project that we're currently working on right now that's essentially just the all-in-one racing intelligence, kind of how Joyce was talking about some of those little things that you might miss during the week. This is a system where you can kind of catch all of it and everything can kind of live in one place. So that's one of the projects we're working on. But really, mainly just racing intelligence tools that allow the crew to assess things through a smarter lens and to make better decisions at the track every weekend.

items.question: What made the experience of racing at Talladega Superspeedway so compelling to you?
items.object: The experience of racing at Talladega Superspeedway
items.answer: So that's kind of the wild, rough-and-rowdy style of race where all your fans from the South have these traditions. At Talladega, you have Talladega Boulevard. So there is a lot more to offer than just the race itself when you go there. So that was a very big event that my mom and dad's friends got involved in, pulled me into it when I was only about five years old. And the moment that I saw the stock cars come down the street, I just knew I was hooked. It was one of those things for me where you get to combine family and friends, and then you have something that's super high-speed that you've never seen before, and the sheer size of that track, and just seeing all these cars going so fast—these guys who are just putting it all out on the line just for competition's sake. Nothing is really more thrilling than that, so that captured me pretty early on.

items.question: How do you see AI tools such as ChatGPT and Codex changing what you can contribute to racing?
items.object: ChatGPT and Codex as tools for contributing to racing
items.answer: I'm a big follower of AI. I've always been interested in science fiction, artificial intelligence. When I was a kid, I would watch Bicentennial Man and A.I. on loop. So the future always really fascinated me. And the moment that a tool like this existed, I knew, okay, I'm about to spend so much time just researching and seeing what's possible. And what can this do? The more I dove into that, the more I started to learn about what the model was capable of. And so I've worked with multiple versions of ChatGPT now, and I'm also working with Codex. But it was the moment for me, understanding that I can now take my ideas and the things that I want to see become real in racing. And I have a way to construct that now. And that was something that I never had before. I remember trying to explain the vision of what I wanted to build to somebody. Sometimes you might hear, “Oh, that's a little far-fetched,” or, “That's a little this.” So I don't have to worry about that now. I can just put that together. I always knew that racing has given so much to me that I want to give back to racing in the way I best can. And for me, that's nothing sweeter than trying to bring something completely new to the sport, something that maybe these guys and girls have never really gotten to experience. And especially just the thought process of looking at the smaller teams or the mid-level teams that don't have as much of that support on the top level. So, putting all of that together, I think it's a big mixture of things—the reason I loved AI so much growing up, without really understanding it. Then, being able to build a career for myself in the racing world, merge those two things, and see that it actually works—I think that was the moment when I was like, “Okay, this is what can allow us to get where we want to go.”

items.question: What draws you to cars and motor racing?
items.answer: I've been into cars for a long time, always fascinated by the combination of engineering, aesthetics, and just kind of the emotional appeal that they have to people. I would say I got into racing—just fell hard for racing during COVID, not because of Drive to Survive, but just because I found myself with time and with a partner who was interested in going to the track with me. And so started going to the track, followed a bunch of different series, everything from sports cars to IndyCar and NASCAR, and just loved the community, loved the engineering, and went from there.

items.question: How did visiting IndyCar team shops shape your thinking about bringing AI into racing?
items.object: Visiting IndyCar team shops and seeing an opportunity for AI in racing
items.answer: I worked in automotive before coming to OpenAI. And being a woman working in this space, I went to this conference just out of curiosity to meet more of the community. And this was out in Indianapolis where most of the IndyCar teams are headquartered. On this trip, the conference organizers had connections to several of the teams who invited us to their shops. This is like an honor. This is like a gift. These teams are usually very secretive. And to be invited in was pretty unusual and really eye-opening for me. It really got me thinking about how the work I do in this AI industry that we are part of can help this sport that I love. We were also really lucky that Chip Ganassi Racing was one of the shops that was part of this conference and they were already looking at how to make AI work for their sport as well. I think this was late 2024.

items.question: Why do you see education about how AI models work as one of your most impactful contributions to the racing team?
items.object: Education about AI models and prompt engineering
items.answer: One of the most impactful things that we've delivered to the team is, frankly, education. It's education about how our models work. I think it helps to pull back the veil and show that these are just machines under the hood, and it's not magic. And these guys are engineers and they understand that. And once you understand how the machine is built, it's easier to conceptualize how to work with them better. So that's taken the form of prompt engineering. But just showing them, for example, that it's all about the input. If you give it the right input, you'll get the output you're looking for. And so there's some onus on you as the user to figure out what that right input is.

items.question: How do you see your role in helping Chip Ganassi prepare for race day?
items.object: Preparation and strategic support for Chip Ganassi
items.answer: Frankly, what we do with Chip Ganassi, we do a lot of prep work ahead of the race day. These guys are just so good at what they do. They know exactly what they need once race day comes. I think we're still exploring what more we could be putting in front of them that would help them with those strategic calls they're making. But a lot of the work we do is ahead of time just to make sure the guys on the timing stand feel as prepped as they possibly can for each and every track.

items.question: Where do you see AI being most useful in helping racing drivers work with their teams?
items.object: AI as a communication aid for racing drivers
items.answer: Driver-wise, I find that the teams are able to put things together. Sometimes you just think these guys, they've been doing this for a long time. They know what they're doing. You're not going to tell them how to do it differently. And they're going to go in there and get that car set up. So you find these other areas where you're like, “Okay, well, when you need me, I'm here for these parts.” But you look at other facets. The driver, I feel like, is a place right now where AI can really help to work more on breaking that communication barrier. Not every driver is an engineer and not every driver understands what is being communicated to them all the time. Sometimes I feel like some drivers will just nod their heads and they might be like, “Sure. Yeah, I understand.” And that's not to say they're not trying to. But I feel like when you're using artificial intelligence now, you're able to hand over something to a driver that may have taken them four to five hours to study and look at. And now you're able to give it to them in a way where it's nice and readable and digestible. And they can figure out exactly what they need to do at the track from a practice report when they're ready to go back out for the actual race and try to get a better finish. So I think on my end, personally, what I've seen is that when the team seems like they've got all the t's crossed and the i's dotted, I'm automatically moving over to the driver. And we have a lot of back-and-forth with that as well on the NASCAR side.

items.question: How do you think people and AI should learn to work together in motorsports?
items.object: People and AI learning to work together in motorsports
items.answer: I think part of the learning is that a lot of the world lives in Excel. The motorsports world definitely lives in Excel. Our models can work with Excel, but it's not their favorite format. So part of it is figuring out—you know, racing, I will say, has a history of the man and the machine. How do you get those to work together as seamlessly as possible? And I think that's one very unique aspect of motorsports in contrast to stick-and-ball sports. And I think AI is part of the machine side of this. It's not just that we need to make AI work with how people work today. It's about having them evolve together and having people learn how to work with and communicate with our models in the most seamless way possible.

items.question: Where do you see the most interesting role for AI in working with motorsports data?
items.object: AI's role in connecting qualitative observations with numerical motorsports data
items.answer: I think the most interesting problems we've been looking at are kind of that soft interface. You have a lot of motorsports data. When we think of data, we think of numbers. We think of telemetry. Well, we've always had scripts. We've had plotting algorithms. We've had all sorts of, I'll call it, traditional software tools to deal with large amounts of data. But then there's all the softer stuff. A driver describes how the car felt. Or how an engineer jots down some notes over the course of a session. That's data too, but that data is harder to organize traditionally. And it's harder to fetch and retrieve, and correlate with these hard-data numbers that we are getting off of the ECUs and other systems. And so one place where AI is really coming in here is to help bridge that gap and coalesce that into a single dataset that people can work with on all sorts of downstream goals.

items.question: How do you see AI tooling giving a time-constrained racing team like Chip Ganassi Racing a competitive edge?
items.object: AI tooling for time-constrained racing teams such as Chip Ganassi Racing
items.answer: I think the thing about AI speeding up what an individual can do is, many of these teams are constrained. The amount of time that they have is limited. And Chip Ganassi is a pretty small outfit in the grand scheme of things. They're under 200 people and everyone wears lots of hats there. And so if any sort of AI tooling or ML tooling that we can build out helps that person do one thing faster or a set of things faster, it frees up their time, it frees up their mind to pursue these questions that they might have been interested in doing, but they got deprioritized. And you never really know. Sometimes those questions that you thought about, but you didn't really have time to look at could be the next big step or the next most revealing thing and the edge that they find in the next race. For a racing team, time is the unit of measure they use for everything. So they're looking at all of their processes. They're looking at, if you think about what an operation it is to get all the stuff that needs to be at the track, to the track, all over the country and sometimes all over the globe for the teams to be able to show up and deliver those results. That's a huge amount of logistics right there. And AI can help with that. It can help with parts tracking. All the parts that fall off the cars, get broken during a race weekend, or need to be replaced—AI can help with that. And so for Chip Ganassi Racing, it's all the way down. They've been looking in every one of their departments for applications where AI can help. Often it's just one individual who needs to be responsible for a ton of different roles and a ton of different projects. They're looking for ways to make AI reduce the most repetitive and most human-error-prone parts of their jobs.

items.question: How do you think about the complexity of racing teams’ spreadsheets when helping them make their data usable by AI?
items.object: Racing teams’ spreadsheet systems and the move toward AI-native data formats
items.answer: When we've been on calls and they pull up these sheets of just tons and tons of data, it feels like they can infinitely scroll to the left or down. And it's a really interesting evolution. There's some joke somewhere that spreadsheets are Turing-complete or something. So you could build anything you want in a spreadsheet. But it really feels like that when you look at some of these. It's the level of complexity of not just the data entry in it, but it's the highlighting. It's the connections. It's the formulas. It just keeps going. And so credit to Chase and RaceTek for trying to figure out how to work natively with that. And to show teams that there is another way to operate with this data. I mean, we've gone through what sounds like a similar process with Chip Ganassi to show them, hey, the investment to convert this into a more AI-native format is worth it because these are all the downstream results you can derive from it if you give the models a format that they can actually work with rather than a format where the model is like, well, sorry. But our models evolve too, so I think it's really important.

items.question: What do you find attractive about the way racing distills your efforts into a result?
items.object: Racing as a distillation of effort, compared with AI research
items.answer: One thing that's really attractive to me about racing is that it's such a distillation of all the things you do. You're looking at the setup, figuring out the exercise regimen for your driver. You're trying to make weather predictions constantly. It's all these things that you're looking at. And at the end of the day, it comes down to a number. And that number is your time or your position and whatnot. It's a really distinct distillation of all your efforts. And I feel that way about a lot of my research, too. You spend months looking at these different datasets, running these different experiments, trying different architectures. And at the end of the day, you're just trying to make the test loss go down. And it's very rewarding to see—well, okay, this test loss is just a number. But when you're doing it at a racetrack, you feel that.

items.question: How do you see AI fitting into human-driven motorsports such as NASCAR and IndyCar?
items.answer: When people talk about the future of AI and robotics, I think sometimes they forget how many of the things we enjoy are enjoyable because they're human-centric. And I think racing is a prime example of that. Maybe there are going to be robot-car races that some people will want to watch. But I don't see IndyCar or NASCAR going away anytime soon. I actually think the application of AI we're seeing in motorsports is extremely human-centric, because these are some of the most goal-oriented people I've ever met and worked with. And when they start working with AI, it's not like, “Lead me. Hey, AI, lead me in this direction.” It's like, “No, I need AI to deliver me this.” And they have a very clear idea of what it needs to be. They have an extremely high-quality bar that needs to be met, and they don't want to waste any time doing that. And so what we have learned working with Chip Ganassi is just how high the performance of our models needs to be to meet that expectation. And it's pushing our models forward and it's allowing them to set goals higher and higher every time. It's very different than just asking the fun questions and exploring what's possible. It is very demanding and you have to make sure that your models are efficient. You have to make sure that whatever you're using delivers the most accurate information possible in real time. items.question: How do you see autonomous racing affecting the appeal of watching human drivers compete?
items.object: Autonomous racing and the appeal of human motorsport
items.answer: I know they do it at Abu Dhabi. They have open-wheel cars where they have a group of engineers that will build an autonomous race car. And they'll try to send them out on these autonomous races. And they're still hitting walls and doing all of those things. But watching where it started in 2022 and where it is now, that's what I feel like a lot of people in racing are thinking when you talk about AI in motorsport. It's like asking, “Are we going to replace basketball players with robots?” No. There will probably be a world for watching a bunch of robots throw a ball around, but I don't think it displaces the one we're in where we want to watch humans perform.

items.question: How do you think AI will change what it takes to find a competitive edge in motorsport?
items.object: Creativity as a competitive advantage in motorsport with AI
items.answer: I think it's going to make creativity so much more important in finding that edge. I think motorsport has gone through cycles where it was just investment. If you invested the resources, the engineering, the effort to build X, then you would find that edge. And now, when the cost of building that is no longer what it was—if you used to need to hire a software engineer and you no longer have to, or you needed to hire any number of specialists—I won't say AI will displace that specialist, but it can get you further in that exploration process of a new idea before you need to pull that specialist in to double-check the work and really fine-tune it. But if you can come up with the idea, you can prove it out yourself much more quickly with the help of AI. And so I'm fascinated to work with the racing experts at Chip Ganassi Racing, see what ideas they're coming up with, and show them, “Hey, you can just build this yourself now.” You don't need to pull all these people in the room just to see if your idea makes sense. You can figure it out, workshop your idea, and then ask, “Of the resources I used to need for this, what do I still need?”
